warmup.q: A nightly job unpacks 1,000 compressed files and exits with code 0. Nothing was logged. The disks have checksums, the network uses TLS, and the servers have ECC memory. How sure can you be that all 1,000 files were unpacked correctly?
options: Certain: checksums and TLS would have caught any corruption
Fairly sure: exit code 0 means every step succeeded
Not sure until something counts or recomputes the output: a CPU or a bug can compute a wrong answer that no layer below the application notices
Certain, because ECC memory corrects bit flips
warmup.why: Checksums and TLS protect bytes stored or sent; ECC repairs flipped bits in memory. None of them can tell that a CPU computed the wrong number. Meta found exactly this: a core that returned 0 for one power calculation, so files were skipped as empty and the job finished normally. An exit code reports that the code ran, not that its answers were right.

sections.h: Disks, CPUs and code can be wrong without saying so
sections.html:
In 2021 Meta published a bug that no test had caught. A Spark job that decompressed files worked out each file's size with a formula that called math.pow. On one core of one CPU, core 59, Int(1.1^53) came out as 0 instead of 156, every time, while 1.1^52 came out right. Files whose size came out as 0 were skipped as empty, the job finished normally, and the database downstream was missing files. Nothing crashed and nothing was logged.

This is silent data corruption, and the What data systems are for track's lesson on faults gave the rate: Meta, Google and Alibaba each report about 1 in 1,000 CPUs that compute wrong results now and then without raising an error. Meta's paper (Dixit and colleagues) ran tests for silent errors across hundreds of thousands of machines and found hundreds of such CPUs. Fault-injection studies had predicted rates orders of magnitude lower.

The layers below the application don't help here, because each one protects something narrower. ECC memory repairs a flipped bit in RAM. TCP checksums and TLS protect bytes on one link. The CRC-32C on a log record, from the Storage engines track's first lesson, catches a torn or flipped record on disk. All of them check that bytes arrived as they were sent. None can tell that the bytes were computed wrongly in the first place, or that the code was wrong.

And the code is wrong often enough. Databases have bugs that break their own promises: MySQL bug #73170 (2014) left duplicates in a unique secondary index, and the authors of the Feral Concurrency Control study found a PostgreSQL bug in 2015 that let duplicates through at serializable isolation. Your own consumers have more: a redelivered message added twice, a catch block that swallows the one record that mattered.

Lesson 3's end-to-end argument applies to integrity as well as to duplicates: a check in a lower layer is an optimization, and only a check at the ends, by code that knows what the data should be, is complete. Storage systems already work this way. HDFS and S3 run background scrubbers that re-read stored data and compare copies, because the only way to know data is still there is to read it back. The same goes for backups: until you have restored one, you don't know that it works.

try.title: A core that computes one number wrong
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It is the shape of Meta's bug, made small: 1,000 files unpacked on 64 cores, and core 59 returns 0 for pow(1.1, 53) and the right answer for everything else.
Before it prints, predict what the job reports, and what the audit at the end reports.
Read the excerpt. Which line would a code review flag? (Probably none: the bug is in the hardware.)

code.title: MercurialCoreDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: private fun pow(core: Int, x: Double, y: Double): Double = if (core == 59 && x == 1.1 && y == 53.0) 0.0 else x.pow(y) // a mercurial core: wrong, and silent val size = pow(core, 1.1, level.toDouble()).toInt() * 4_096 if (size == 0) continue // "nothing to unpack"

try.expect:
job: unpacked 999 files, exit code 0, no errors logged
audit: 1000 files in, 999 files out, 1 missing
  file 59: level 53, unpacked on core 59
pow(1.1, 53) on a good core = 156, on core 59 = 0

The job reports success, because from its point of view it succeeded: every step ran and nothing threw. Only the count at the end, files in against files out, notices the gap, and the details point straight at one core and one input. The demo's numbers are invented; the mechanism is the one in Meta's paper.

MySQL bug #73170: duplicates in a unique secondary index

sections.h: Design for auditability: an immutable log and derivations you can rerun
sections.html:
You can only audit what you can recompute. If a balances table is updated in place by code that reads requests, calls other services and writes results, there is no second opinion. The only record of what the table should contain is the table.

The design this track keeps returning to fixes that. The log is the system of record and is never changed. Every view is a deterministic function of the log: the same log in, the same view out. That is what the What data systems are for track's first lesson meant by derived data: something you can always rebuild from the record. So an audit job can replay the log from offset 0 into a fresh view, compare it key by key with the live view, and treat every difference as a bug somewhere between the two.

Rerunnable has a price. The derivation can't read the wall clock, draw random numbers or ask a service whose answer changes from one call to the next. Put the exchange rate, the fee schedule version and the event time into the event, and the audit gets the same inputs the live consumer had.

The lab's live consumer keeps a balance per account from a 5,000-posting ledger log, and each run injects one silent bug. The recomputed view finds all of them, and each leaves its own fingerprint:

Bug in the live consumer Accounts off Total drift (cents) Grand totals match?
swallows every 1,000th record 5 -12,056 no
redelivers offsets 10 to 12 after a crash 3 +8,420 no
one bit flipped in one stored balance 1 +1,048,576 (2^20) no
two flips that cancel 2 0 yes
cents cut off from offset 2,500 497 -44,780 no

Dropped records leave accounts short by exactly the dropped amounts. A redelivery leaves them over by exactly the replayed ones. A flipped bit leaves one account off by a power of two, a signature of hardware rather than logic. Truncation touches nearly every account, each by less than a unit per posting.

Look at the last column. Comparing grand totals, a reconciliation, is cheap and caught four of the five, but two errors that cancel sail through. Sum and count checks make good alarms that can run every minute. Only the key-by-key recompute is an audit. Run it often enough that a bug is found while the log still holds the data you need to repair it, and keep the log for at least that long. The same replay also repairs: fix the consumer, rebuild the view as a new version next to the old one, as lesson 1 did, and switch.

try.title: Find five silent bugs by recomputing
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It runs the live consumer six times, once with no fault and once with each injected bug, and audits each run.
Predict before it prints: which bug will the grand-total check miss? Which one changes the most accounts?
Look at the last column. Which bug makes the Merkle comparison expensive, and why? The next section explains.

code.title: AuditDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: val live = liveBalances(log, *faults) val drift = diff(live, truth) // key by key: the audit val totalsMatch = live.values.sum() == truth.values.sum() // one number: the alarm val m = compare(MerkleTree(truth), MerkleTree(live)) // 1,024 key ranges

try.expect:
fault                                   accounts off   total drift   totals match   merkle comparisons
no fault                                            0             0            yes                    1
drop every 1,000th record                           5        -12056             NO                   85
redeliver offsets 10..12 after a crash              3          8420             NO                   53
flip bit 20 of acct-123                             1       1048576             NO                   21
two flips that cancel in the total                  2             0            yes                   39
truncate cents from offset 2,500                  497        -44780             NO                 1599

The total check misses the two flips that cancel: one account went up by 16 cents and another down by 16. Truncation changes 497 of 500 accounts, and that is also the run where the Merkle comparison costs more (1,599) than looking at all 1,024 ranges, because almost every range differs.

sections.h: A Merkle tree finds the drift without comparing every row
sections.html:
Recomputing is the easy half. In production the live view might be 50 million rows in the serving database, and the recomputed one sits in the warehouse. Comparing them row by row means moving 50 million rows across the network every time you audit.

The Replication track's lesson on leaderless replication met the same problem between replicas, and the same tool answers it: a Merkle tree. Cut the key space into 2^k ranges by a hash of the key. Each leaf is the hash of every entry in its range, in key order. Each parent is the hash of its two children, up to one root. Equal roots mean equal views, as far as SHA-256 can tell, and an accidental collision is not a practical worry. Different roots mean something differs, and the tree says where.

Compare the roots. If they differ, compare the two children, and only go down into a child that differs. One bad key in 1,024 ranges costs 1 + 2 x 10 = 21 comparisons, the root and then two children at each of ten levels, instead of 1,024 range comparisons or 50 million row comparisons. Then you diff rows only inside the range that was found. Each side builds its tree where its data lives, and only hashes cross the network until that last step.

The cost grows with the number of bad ranges, not the size of the view. The lab's numbers, for accounts with one flipped bit:

Bad accounts 256 ranges 1,024 ranges 4,096 ranges
1 17 21 25
3 43 53 65
10 101 147 185
100 369 717 1,137

With 100 bad accounts in 256 ranges, the tree did more comparisons (369) than there are ranges. When most ranges differ, a scan is cheaper, and you have one big bug, not a hundred small ones, so a sample of a few ranges is enough to find it.

Merkle trees turn up wherever two copies of something big must be compared cheaply: Cassandra's repair between replicas, Git's commits, and the transparency logs in the next section.

sections.h: A hash chain proves the log wasn't rewritten, if someone else holds its head
sections.html:
The audit trusts the log. So what if the log itself changes: a disk corrupts an old segment, or someone with access edits a posting from last month?

A hash chain makes any change to history visible. Each entry stores the hash of the previous entry, and its own hash covers that link and its payload: hash = SHA-256(prev + payload). Edit entry 412 and its stored hash no longer matches its contents. A verifier that recomputes the chain from the start stops at exactly 412. That catches careless edits and corruption.

It doesn't catch an insider who controls the whole log. They can edit entry 412 and recompute every hash after it, and the chain is consistent with itself again. The defence is to publish the head, the newest entry's hash, somewhere the log's owner can't change it: send it to the auditors every night, write it into another organization's log, print it in the settlement report the bank countersigns. A verifier holding yesterday's head notices a rewritten history, and also a log with its newest entries cut off. The lab builds all three attacks.

Transparency logs scale the idea to logs the whole internet can check. The log keeps a Merkle tree over its entries and signs the root. Anyone can ask for an inclusion proof (this entry is in the tree, shown with about log2(n) hashes) or a consistency proof (today's tree contains yesterday's unchanged). Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962 in 2013, version 2.0 in RFC 9162 in 2021) logs every publicly trusted TLS certificate. Chrome and Safari require certificates to carry signed timestamps from logs, and monitors scan the logs for certificates issued for their domains that they didn't ask for. There is no blockchain: each log has one writer, and other parties keep it honest by checking. Sigstore's Rekor does the same for software signatures; its version 2 is a tile-based log, released as rekor-tiles (v2.4.1 in October 2026).

Ledger databases package a hash-chained journal as a product. Amazon QLDB was one, and AWS discontinued it on 31 July 2025, recommending Aurora PostgreSQL, which keeps no immutable history of its own. immudb (v1.11.2 in September 2026) is an open-source alternative. The lesson from QLDB is to build audit trails on mechanisms you can take with you: hash chains, Merkle proofs and logs you can export. And remember what any of them proves. A chained or signed log shows the entries weren't changed after they were written. It can't show that the right entries were written in the first place. That is the recompute audit's job, and the boundary checks' in the next section.

try.title: Three attacks on a hash-chained log
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It builds a chain of 1,000 postings, keeps its head as "published", then attacks three fresh copies.
Predict each pair of answers: verify() checks the chain against itself, verify(published) also compares the head. null means it found nothing wrong.
Which attack would a disk failure look like, and which one needs a person?

code.title: Model.kt (excerpt)
code.html: for (e in entries) { if (!e.prev.contentEquals(expectedPrev)) return e.index // a broken link if (!e.hash.contentEquals(sha256(e.prev, e.payload.toByteArray()))) return e.index // edited payload expectedPrev = e.hash } if (publishedHead != null && !head.contentEquals(publishedHead)) return size // rewritten or cut short

try.expect:
published head: f51e37f4efa835a8...
edit entry 412 in place:          verify() = 412, verify(published) = 412
edit 412 and recompute the rest:  verify() = null, verify(published) = 1000
drop the last 100 entries:        verify() = null, verify(published) = 900

An edit in place, which is what corruption on disk looks like, fails the self-check at exactly entry 412. The other two attacks need someone who controls the log: recomputing every later hash, or cutting off the newest entries. The chain alone can't see either. Only the head published before the attack can, and it reports where the published history and this one part ways.

sections.h: Check data where it crosses a boundary: quality checks and contracts
sections.html:
Many integrity bugs don't start in your system. They arrive. A producer team starts sending amounts in whole units instead of cents, or renames merchant_id, or sends nulls for a week, and every consumer derives wrong data from it without a single error. The Encoding, APIs and workflows track's schema rules check the shape of a record, and an int64 amount in cents and an int64 amount in units have the same shape.

A data quality check is an assertion about data, run like a test. A few kinds catch most problems. Validity checks look at single values: not null, unique, in the allowed set, in a sane range (a card payment between 0.01 and 50,000.00). Referential checks make sure every payment's merchant exists. Freshness checks ask whether the newest event is less than an hour old. Volume checks compare today's row count with the same day last week. Reconciliation checks that the day's payouts add up to the day's ledger postings. dbt has the first kinds built in as data tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships), which run after a model is built and return the rows that break them. Its model contracts go one step earlier: with contract: enforced: true, the build fails if the model's columns and types don't match what was declared.

A data contract writes down what the producer promises and the consumer relies on, so machines can check it: the schema, what each field means and in which units, allowed values, freshness and volume targets, and who owns it. The Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS), from the Bitol project at the Linux Foundation, is a YAML format for these; its site lists version 3.2.0. A contract only helps if something runs it, in the producer's CI before a change ships and at the consumer before data is used.

Where checks run matters as much as what they check. At the producer, before publishing, a failure is cheapest to fix. At the consumer, before deriving, a check protects your views from someone else's bug. On outputs, before anything irreversible, a check is the last line: reconcile the settlement file against the ledger before it goes to the bank. And when a check fails, stop the line. Quarantine the batch, page someone, and keep the bad data out of the views, because a check that only logs a warning is the catch block that swallows the record all over again.

try.title: Write the checks for a settlement table
steps: A table settlement_lines has one row per payout: payout_id, merchant_id, amount_cents, currency, settled_on. It is built every night from the ledger and sent to the bank in the morning.
Write down five checks, at least one of each kind: validity, referential, freshness or volume, and reconciliation. For each, say what bug it would catch.
Decide which ones must pass before the file goes to the bank, and what the job should do when one fails.
try.expect:
One reasonable set, in dbt-style YAML plus one SQL check (yours will differ):

models:
  - name: settlement_lines
    columns:
      - name: payout_id
        data_tests: [unique, not_null]          # a payout sent twice, or with no id
      - name: merchant_id
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              arguments: {to: ref('merchants'), field: merchant_id}   # a payout to nobody
      - name: currency
        data_tests:
          - accepted_values:
              arguments: {values: ['EUR', 'GBP', 'USD']}

-- reconciliation: returns a row (a failure) if the file and the ledger disagree
SELECT s.total, l.total
FROM (SELECT sum(amount_cents) AS total FROM settlement_lines WHERE settled_on = :day) s,
     (SELECT sum(cents) AS total FROM ledger_postings WHERE kind = 'payout' AND day = :day) l
WHERE s.total <> l.total;

Add a volume check (row count within 30% of the same weekday last week) to catch a half-built file, and a range check on amount_cents to catch the units-for-cents change. The uniqueness, reconciliation and volume checks must pass before sending, because the bank can't un-send money. On failure the job keeps the file back, pages the on-call engineer and leaves yesterday's state in place. It never sends a file "with warnings".

analogy: A bank branch counting its cash at closing. The tellers' ledger says what should be in the vault, and someone counts the notes and compares, trusting neither the tellers nor the cash machine's own counter. Counting by bundles is the Merkle tree: if a bundle's total matches, don't count its notes, and if one bundle is off, count only that one. The numbered, carbon-copied deposit slips are the hash chain: tear one out and the gap shows, and the copies sent to head office are the published head. The analogy breaks on speed and scale. A branch counts once a day by hand, while a data system can recompute and compare its views every hour. And an insider can rewrite a digital slip book in a second, which is why its head must be held by someone else.
world: Payments teams already audit, often by hand: the daily reconciliation of the ledger against the processor's settlement file, and of payouts against bank statements. Turn it into a job that runs every hour from the Kafka topic: replay the day's postings into a fresh balance map and diff it per merchant against the Oracle table, and alert on any difference, however small. Keep the Kafka consumers rerunnable by putting the FX rate and the fee schedule version into the event instead of looking them up when the event is consumed. Hash-chain the ledger postings (the previous hash in a column, computed in the same transaction as the insert) and send the daily head to your auditors or to an account they control. Put checks on the settlement table, with dbt or plain SQL: unique payout IDs, no null merchants, totals equal to the ledger, before the file goes out. And restore the Oracle backup and replay the topic into a scratch schema on a schedule. A backup nobody has restored is only a guess.
mistake: Trusting the layers below: "the disks are RAID with checksums, the network is TLS, Kafka has CRCs and the database is ACID, so our balances are right." Each of those protects bytes in one place against one kind of fault. None of them checks that the right computation produced the bytes, and none of them can see a bug in your consumer. The fix is a check at the application level, end to end: recompute derived views from the log and diff them, reconcile totals at every boundary, and read data back, backups included, to prove it is still there. The second mistake is reconciling only totals. Two errors that cancel pass a sum check, so treat sums and counts as alarms and the per-key recompute as the audit.

compare.title: A reconciliation and an audit

a.label: Reconciliation
a.title: one number per side
a.html: -- cheap, runs every minute; misses errors that cancel SELECT (SELECT sum(cents) FROM ledger_postings WHERE day = :day) AS from_log, (SELECT sum(delta) FROM balance_changes WHERE day = :day) AS from_view;

b.label: Recompute and diff
b.title: every key
b.html: // replay the log into a fresh view, then compare key by key val expected = sortedMapOf<String, Long>() for (p in log) expected[p.account] = (expected[p.account] ?: 0L) + p.cents val drift = (live.keys + expected.keys).toSortedSet() .filter { live[it] != expected[it] } .map { Drift(it, live[it], expected[it]) }

compare.note: The reconciliation compares two numbers and costs almost nothing, so it can run constantly as an alarm. It can't say which account is wrong, and two errors of opposite sign cancel in it. The recompute costs a replay of the log and a comparison per key, and it finds every difference and its size, which is what you need to repair the view. Use the first as the smoke detector and the second as the inspection, with a Merkle tree in between when the two views live far apart.

worked.title: Verify a three-entry hash chain by hand

steps.say: Entry 0 links to the genesis hash, 32 zero bytes. Its hash covers that link and its payload. (Hashes are real SHA-256 values, cut to 12 hex digits.)
Each later entry stores the previous hash as its prev. The last hash is the head, and it goes to the auditors.
steps.code:
hash1 = sha256(hash0 + "1,acct-123,-400") = 868b50f834cd...
hash2 = sha256(hash1 + "2,acct-007,9999") = 1fe40a4c193a...
published head = 1fe40a4c193a...

steps.say: Someone edits entry 1 from -400 to -40 and leaves the hashes alone. The verifier recomputes entry 1's hash and compares it with the stored one.
steps.code:
sha256(hash0 + "1,acct-123,-40") = e9b57bd3945e...
stored hash1                      = 868b50f834cd...   -> mismatch: verify() = 1

steps.say: An insider does better: edits entry 1 and recomputes hash1 and hash2, so every link checks out again.
steps.code:
hash1' = e9b57bd3945e...   entry 2's prev = hash1'
hash2' = 37f55def423f...   verify() = null (consistent with itself)

steps.say: The published head catches it. The chain's head is now hash2', and the auditors hold the old one.

lab.title: Audit a derived view: recompute it, Merkle-diff it, hash-chain its log
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. 19 tests run and all fail with NotImplementedError. Ledger.kt is finished: the seeded ledger log, the live consumer, and its four injectable faults.
In Audit.kt, write recompute and diff. Run AuditTest: each fault test checks the fingerprint the bug should leave, such as accounts short by exactly the dropped amounts.
In Merkle.kt, write buildInternalNodes and compare. Run MerkleTest. The 21-comparison test fails if your walk looks at children of nodes that already match.
In HashChain.kt, write append and verify. Run HashChainTest, and note which two attacks only the published head catches.
If you have time, add a fault to Ledger.kt of your own, such as postings for acct-007 applied to acct-070, and predict its fingerprint before you diff.
hints: recompute: for (p in log) view[p.account] = (view[p.account] ?: 0L) + p.cents, with view a sortedMapOf.
diff: take (live.keys + expected.keys).toSortedSet(), keep the keys where live[it] != expected[it], and map each to a Drift.

compare: a local recursive fun visit(node: Int) that counts, returns on equal hashes, records node - leaves for a leaf, and otherwise visits 2 * node then 2 * node + 1. Compare byte arrays with contentEquals, never ==.
verify: keep expectedPrev, starting at GENESIS. Check the link, then the hash, then move expectedPrev on. Compare the head with publishedHead only after the loop.

drill.title: Audits from memory
drill.prompt: Without notes: (1) write compare for two Merkle trees stored as arrays (root at 1, children at 2i and 2i + 1, leaves from leaves on); (2) give the number of comparisons for one bad key with 2^k ranges; (3) name what a hash chain catches on its own, and the two attacks that need a published head; (4) say why a grand-total reconciliation is not an audit.

answer.html: // (1) fun compare(a: MerkleTree, b: MerkleTree): MerkleDiff { val found = ArrayList<Int>() var n = 0 fun visit(node: Int) { n++ if (a.nodes[node].contentEquals(b.nodes[node])) return if (node >= a.leaves) { found += node - a.leaves; return } visit(2 * node); visit(2 * node + 1) } visit(1) return MerkleDiff(found, n) } // (2) 1 + 2k: the root, then two children at each of k levels (21 for 1,024 ranges) // (3) alone: any entry edited in place (corruption, careless edits), at its index; // with a published head: a rewrite that recomputes every later hash, and truncation // (4) errors of opposite sign cancel in a sum, and a total can't say which key is wrong

recap: Hardware, databases and your own code produce wrong data without raising errors: about 1 in 1,000 CPUs at hyperscalers, and Meta's core 59 returned 0 for 1.1^53. Checksums, TLS and ECC protect bytes in one place, not the computation.

Design for auditability: an immutable log plus derivations that depend only on it lets a job recompute any view and diff it key by key. Each bug leaves a fingerprint; total reconciliations are alarms, not audits.
A Merkle tree compares two big views by exchanging hashes: 1 + 2 log2(n) comparisons for one bad range, then a row diff of that range only.

A hash chain catches edits to history on its own; a head published where the owner can't change it also catches rewrites and truncation. Transparency logs (Certificate Transparency, Rekor) scale this with Merkle proofs; QLDB's end of life argues for portable mechanisms.

Check data where it crosses boundaries: validity, referential, freshness, volume and reconciliation checks, and data contracts both sides run. A failed check stops the line before anything irreversible.

explain.prompt: Your manager asks why the team should spend time on an audit job when "the database is ACID, the disks are replicated and Kafka has checksums." Explain what those guarantee, what they don't, and what the audit adds.
explain.answer: Each of those protects bytes against one kind of fault in one place. ACID makes our transactions atomic and isolated, replication survives a dead disk, and Kafka's CRCs catch a corrupted record. None of them checks that the numbers we wrote were the right numbers. A consumer that applies a redelivered posting twice writes a perfectly valid, perfectly replicated, correctly checksummed wrong balance. A CPU can compute a wrong value without any error, which Meta and Google see in about 1 in 1,000 CPUs. And databases have bugs too, such as a MySQL bug that left duplicates in a unique index. The audit job is the end-to-end check: it replays the immutable log into a fresh view and compares it with the live one, account by account, so any drift is found while the log still has what we need to fix it. A Merkle tree makes that comparison cheap across systems. A hash chain with a head we send to the auditors proves the log itself wasn't changed.

deeper.html:
Mercurial cores at Google. In the same year as Meta's paper, Google's "Cores that don't count" (Hochschild and colleagues, HotOS 2021) described CPU cores that occasionally compute wrong results, which they called mercurial, and reported seeing a few per several thousand machines. Both companies now run test suites for silent errors across their fleets and take suspect cores out of service. You can't run their tests, but you can run their idea: for important computations, compute twice on different machines and compare.

How transparency logs stay cheap. A Certificate Transparency log promises to add each certificate within its maximum merge delay, usually 24 hours, and returns a signed timestamp at once. Monitors download new entries and check them, and anyone who has seen two signed tree heads can ask for a consistency proof that the later tree extends the earlier one. A log that shows different trees to different people is caught as soon as two of them compare heads, which is why gossip between monitors matters. Newer logs serve the tree as static tiles, files that any web cache can serve, which is the design behind Rekor v2.

Reads are events too. If a fraud decision depends on what a model saw, log what it saw: the features, the model version and the score, with the decision's request ID. Then an audit can recompute the decision as well as the balance, and the next lesson shows why that record matters to people who want to contest a decision.

The argument for auditing derived data end to end is made in Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 13.
